title: Theoretical derivation 177: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 177)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. Each worked entry evaluates the defining sum directly, then re-derives the same answer through a property shortcut, because agreement between the two routes is the strongest available check.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 177)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: y(t) = integral x(tau) h(t-tau) dtau ; y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 177 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.

title: Theoretical derivation 177: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 177)

title: Theoretical derivation 177: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 177)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. Difference equations become rational H(z) by term-by-term transformation, and inverse transforms are checked by power-series expansion so that algebra and sequence agree coefficient by coefficient.

For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Theoretical derivation 177: Waves, Channels & Data-Rate Limits — worked from first principles (parameter set 177)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 179: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 179)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Modulation moves information onto a carrier by varying amplitude, frequency or phase, and digital keying quantises that variation into constellation points. These derivations expand AM products into carrier and sideband terms with power accounted watt by watt, apply bandwidth rules (double-sideband, Carson for FM) with their assumptions stated, and convert between baud and bit rate through bits per symbol, always returning to the constellation picture where distance between points explains noise immunity better than any slogan.

The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. title: Theoretical derivation 183: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 183)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. title: Formal proof-style derivation 188: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 188)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. The derivations in this module therefore always begin by naming the class, then applying the class-specific integral or sum, then checking the result against the defining property.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 188)

title: Theoretical derivation 189: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 189)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. title: Formal proof-style derivation 191: Elementary Signals & Operations — worked from first principles (parameter set 191)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Elementary signals are the atoms of the subject. The impulse extracts values through sifting, the step accumulates impulse area, the ramp accumulates the step, and exponentials rotate and scale through Euler's identity. title: Theoretical derivation 195: Systems & LTI Properties — worked from first principles (parameter set 195)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. title: Numerical derivation 202: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 202)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 202)

State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. The derivations here build (A, B, C, D) from differential or difference equations, solve through (sI minus A) inverse or A-to-the-n evolution, and read stability from eigenvalues of A, closing the loop with Modules 5 and 6 because H(s) equals C (sI minus A) inverse B plus D and the eigenvalues are exactly the system poles.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 203)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: xdot = A x + B u ; y = C x + D u ; H(s) = C(sI-A)^{-1} B + D. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 203 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. title: Numerical derivation 205: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 205)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION

title: Numerical derivation 208: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 208)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. The derivations in this module therefore always begin by naming the class, then applying the class-specific integral or sum, then checking the result against the defining property.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 208)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 209: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 209)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. Derivations here compute coefficients from the integral definition, verify power in both domains, and interpret magnitude and phase spectra as instructions for what a filter will do.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 209)

title: Numerical derivation 211: Elementary Signals & Operations — worked from first principles (parameter set 211)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Elementary signals are the atoms of the subject. The impulse extracts values through sifting, the step accumulates impulse area, the ramp accumulates the step, and exponentials rotate and scale through Euler's identity. Every complicated waveform in later modules is assembled from shifted, folded and scaled copies of these atoms, so each derivation here isolates one operation, performs it symbolically first, and only then substitutes numbers, keeping sign and shift errors visible rather than hiding them inside arithmetic.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Numerical derivation, parameter set 211)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: integral x(t) delta(t-t0) dt = x(t0) ; u(t) = integral_{-inf}^{t} delta ; e^{jwt} = cos wt + j sin wt. title: Formal proof-style derivation 212: DT Fourier, DFT & Sampling — worked from first principles (parameter set 212)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. The derivations in this module pass carefully between DFS, DTFT and DFT instead of conflating them, evaluate small DFTs directly from the definition sum, and treat the sampling theorem as a geometric statement about spectral copies: recovery is possible exactly when the copies do not overlap, and the anti-alias filter is what enforces that precondition.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 212)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Communication channels are governed by two complementary laws. Shannon's capacity, built from bandwidth and SNR, is an upper bound no coding can exceed in noise; Nyquist's formula turns a chosen rate into required signal levels on a noiseless channel. Derivations here convert decibels carefully, compute capacities with every logarithm shown, and then chain the two laws in the engineering order: Shannon first for feasibility, a practical rate below it, Nyquist last for levels and baud, finishing with attenuation and SNR bookkeeping in dB.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 215)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: C = B log2(1+SNR) ; BitRate = 2B log2(L) ; dB = 10 log10(P2/P1). Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 215 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Formal proof-style derivation 215: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 215)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u. title: Theoretical derivation 216: Systems & LTI Properties — worked from first principles (parameter set 216)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. Equality for all inputs proves the property; a single counterexample disproves it, which is why each derivation ends with an explicit verdict and the boundary case that would change it.

title: Formal proof-style derivation 218: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 218)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. title: Theoretical derivation 219: Modulation & Transmission — worked from first principles (parameter set 219)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Modulation moves information onto a carrier by varying amplitude, frequency or phase, and digital keying quantises that variation into constellation points. The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: X(s) = integral x(t) e^{-st} dt ; H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) ; poles in LHP for causal stability. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. Difference equations become rational H(z) by term-by-term transformation, and inverse transforms are checked by power-series expansion so that algebra and sequence agree coefficient by coefficient.

title: Formal proof-style derivation 227: Signals & Classification — worked from first principles (parameter set 227)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A signal is information made measurable: a function of time whose shape can be classified before any system touches it. Classification is not taxonomy for its own sake; each class selects the correct mathematics. Periodic signals invite Fourier series, finite-energy signals invite the Fourier transform, and discrete-time signals force the periodicity question to pass through rationality of Omega0 over 2 pi. The derivations in this module therefore always begin by naming the class, then applying the class-specific integral or sum, then checking the result against the defining property.

title: Theoretical derivation 228: Fourier Series & Transform (CT) — worked from first principles (parameter set 228)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Elementary signals are the atoms of the subject. The impulse extracts values through sifting, the step accumulates impulse area, the ramp accumulates the step, and exponentials rotate and scale through Euler's identity. Every complicated waveform in later modules is assembled from shifted, folded and scaled copies of these atoms, so each derivation here isolates one operation, performs it symbolically first, and only then substitutes numbers, keeping sign and shift errors visible rather than hiding them inside arithmetic.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 230)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: integral x(t) delta(t-t0) dt = x(t0) ; u(t) = integral_{-inf}^{t} delta ; e^{jwt} = cos wt + j sin wt. Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 230 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

title: Formal proof-style derivation 230: Systems & LTI Properties — worked from first principles (parameter set 230)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 230: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 230)

title: Formal proof-style derivation 230: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 230)

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. title: Formal proof-style derivation 230: z-Transform & DT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 230)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. These derivations emphasise the geometry: right-sided sequences converge outside their outermost pole, stability demands that the ROC include the unit circle, and causal stability collapses to the memorable picture of poles inside the circle. title: Numerical derivation 238: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 238)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. Modulation moves information onto a carrier by varying amplitude, frequency or phase, and digital keying quantises that variation into constellation points. These derivations expand AM products into carrier and sideband terms with power accounted watt by watt, apply bandwidth rules (double-sideband, Carson for FM) with their assumptions stated, and convert between baud and bit rate through bits per symbol, always returning to the constellation picture where distance between points explains noise immunity better than any slogan.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Formal proof-style derivation, parameter set 239)
Step 1 — State the governing relation. For this module the derivation is anchored on: s_AM = Ac[1+mu m(t)] cos(wc t) ; BW_AM = 2 BWm ; BitRate = Baud x log2(L). Every symbol is defined before use, units are carried, and no result is quoted without the relation that produces it.
Step 2 — Fix the parameter set. Parameter set 239 selects the numerical constants appearing in the evidence table below (derived deterministically from the set index, so this derivation can be regenerated and audited). Record the givens, the target quantity, and the model assumptions before any algebra.
Step 3 — Apply the definition literally. Substitute the entry's signal/system into the defining integral, sum, or transform — do not start from a memorised shortcut. Shortcuts are used only in Step 6 as an independent cross-check.
Step 4 — Evaluate in stages. Break the evaluation into the rows of the evidence table: each row is one abscissa (time, index, frequency, SNR, or bin), the quantity evaluated there, and a running or closed-form comparator evaluated in parallel.
Step 5 — Take the limit or closed form. Where the table accumulates (energy, partial sums, partial Fourier sums, convolution running sums), compare the accumulation against its closed form or limit and note the convergence behaviour explicitly.
Step 6 — Cross-check by an independent route. Re-derive the headline result through the module's property shortcut (symmetry, Parseval, convolution properties, pole location, Shannon-then-Nyquist ordering, or eigenvalue equivalence) and require agreement with Step 4.
Step 7 — Interrogate boundary cases. Ask what changes at the edges of validity: a pole crossing an axis or circle, fs falling below twice fm, mu exceeding 1, a non-rational Omega0 over 2 pi, or an ROC that excludes the stability contour. State the verdict change in one sentence.
Step 8 — Interpret physically. Translate the mathematics back into the system story: what decays, what rings, what folds, what saturates, and what a measurement would actually show.

CONCEPT AND INTUITION
A system is a rule that maps inputs to outputs, and the five property tests (memory, causality, linearity, time-invariance, stability) are procedures, not adjectives. The formal pattern in this module is always the same: assume two arbitrary inputs and their outputs, form a combined or shifted input, push it through the rule, and compare against the required combination or shift of outputs. The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The z-transform is the discrete-time mirror of Laplace, with the unit circle playing the role of the jw axis. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Fourier analysis re-expresses signals in the basis of eternal exponentials. For periodic signals the spectrum is a line spectrum whose coefficients come from one-period integrals and obey symmetry shortcuts and Parseval power bookkeeping; for aperiodic signals the transform is a density and convolution becomes multiplication, which is the entire basis of filtering. CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Discrete-time spectra are periodic with period 2 pi, finite data produce the DFT's N bins, and sampling replicates spectra every fs so that overlap becomes aliasing. title: Formal proof-style derivation 257: Convolution & LTI Response — worked from first principles (parameter set 257)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
Convolution is the LTI engine: decompose the input into impulses, answer each impulse with a shifted impulse response, and sum. The derivations here move between the integral or sum definition, the graphical flip-shift-multiply-accumulate reading, and the algebraic properties (commutativity, distributivity, associativity) that let engineers reorder and merge systems. title: Theoretical derivation 261: Laplace Transform & CT Systems — worked from first principles (parameter set 261)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
The Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebra and, crucially, carries a region of convergence that decides which time signal a given X(s) means. Derivations in this module therefore never quote X(s) alone: poles, zeros and ROC are derived together, partial fractions are inverted term by term with the ROC selecting right- or left-sided inverses, and stability is read from pole positions relative to the jw axis. The unilateral form additionally converts initial conditions into sources, which is what makes circuit problems mechanical.

FORMAL DERIVATION (Theoretical derivation, parameter set 261)

title: Numerical derivation 262: State-Space Analysis — worked from first principles (parameter set 262)
body:
CONCEPT AND INTUITION
State-space models package a system's memory into a state vector so that dynamics become matrix algebra: x-dot equals A x plus B u, y equals C x plus D u.
